hints: A clean rollback needs nothing beyond redeploying the previous code. Does each of these leave anything else changed that the old code can't undo on its own?
explanation: The two 'not clean' cases both destroy something (a column, an old structure) in the same step that starts relying on its replacement — redeploying old code afterward has nothing to read, because what it needs no longer exists. The two clean cases never destroy anything the old code depended on, so reverting the code alone is sufficient.

prompt: A proposed deploy ships a new required field in a message queue payload, with producer and consumer deployed in the same release but rolling out independently. What determines the actual risk here?

options.text: Whether the field is treated as optional/tolerated until every producer and consumer instance has rolled out
Whether the message queue software is up to date
How many total messages are sent per day
Whether the release notes mention the change

hints: Same release doesn't mean same instant — what happens during the window where some instances are old and some are new?
explanation: The risk lives entirely in the rollout window where old and new instances of producer and consumer are simultaneously live — a required field that either side isn't ready for yet breaks messages exactly during that window, regardless of how the release is documented or how much traffic there is. Treating the field as optional until rollout is fully complete removes the risk.

prompt: A risky new payment-retry behaviour is being shipped behind a feature flag, defaulting off, with a plan to enable it for 1% of traffic first. True or false: this deploy's rollback story is meaningfully better than shipping the same code live to 100% of traffic immediately.

config.statement: Shipping risky new behaviour behind a feature flag with a gradual rollout gives a meaningfully better rollback story than shipping it live to everyone immediately.
config.rubric: Accepts justification naming that the flag lets a bad behaviour be turned off instantly via config rather than requiring a code deploy to revert, and limits blast radius to 1% while it's being validated.

hints: If something goes wrong at 1%, what's the fastest way back to safety — with the flag, versus without it?
explanation: Yes — the flag turns 'undo this' into a config change instead of a code deploy, which is faster and lower-risk, and the 1% rollout limits how many people are affected while the behaviour is still being validated. This is the concrete version of feature flags' value from the lesson: separating deploy from release buys a faster, cheaper undo specifically for the class of bug that only shows up with real traffic.

prompt: A proposed deploy runs a one-time script that deletes all rows in an `abandoned_carts` table older than 90 days, as "cleanup," with no backup taken first. Judge its rollback story and state what would make it acceptable.
hints: Once rows are deleted with no backup, what does 'undo this' even mean?
What would need to exist beforehand for this to be an acceptable operation?
explanation: As described, this has no rollback story at all — deleted rows with no backup are simply gone, and 'redeploy the old code' does nothing to bring back data. This is a genuinely destructive, irreversible operation, and it becomes acceptable only with a real precaution beforehand: an export or backup of the rows being deleted, taken and verified before the delete runs, so 'undo this' has an actual answer if the 90-day cutoff turns out to be wrong or the data is needed after all.

prompt: A generated onboarding-email function logs console.log("sending email") before sending and console.log("email sent") after. A customer reports never receiving their welcome email. What's the single biggest gap in these two lines for diagnosing that report?

options.text: Neither line names which customer, which email address, or which template — there's nothing to search on for this specific customer's complaint
The lines should say "Sending email..." with an ellipsis for clarity
Two log lines isn't enough — the function needs at least five
console.log doesn't support async functions

hints: The customer's complaint is specific to them — could you find their email among every 'email sent' line ever logged?
What field, if present, would let you search directly for this customer's attempt?
explanation: The count of log lines and their wording aren't the problem — the problem is that neither line contains anything to search on. A reader with "customer X never got their email" has no field to filter by; every occurrence of both lines is identical text. An identifier — customerId, recipientEmail, templateId — is what turns this into a debuggable line instead of a generic confirmation that some email, at some point, was sent to someone.

prompt: A team rewrites console.log("payment failed") as log.warn("payment.declined", { paymentId, customerId, providerCode }). True or false: the main benefit of this change is that warn-level logs are stored longer than info-level logs.

config.statement: The main benefit of rewriting a free-text log line into a structured one with named fields is that it changes the log's storage retention period.
config.rubric: Accepts justification naming that the benefit is searchability/queryability of the individual field values (paymentId, customerId, providerCode), not retention — retention is governed by log level and storage policy, a separate and unrelated axis from whether the payload is structured.

hints: What changed between the two versions — is it the log level, or the shape of the data?
Would a reader searching for a specific paymentId be able to find it in the first version? The second?
explanation: Retention policy is typically set by log level and storage configuration, and is unrelated to whether a payload is structured or free text — you could have a structured info-level log with short retention, or an unstructured warn-level log with long retention. The actual benefit of the rewrite is that paymentId, customerId, and providerCode are now individually searchable and filterable fields instead of words buried inside a sentence, which is what lets a reader actually find this specific payment among thousands of others.

prompt: A generated function logs logger.info(`User ${userId} changed email from ${oldEmail} to ${newEmail}`). Beyond the string-interpolation problem, what's the separate issue with this specific line?

options.text: It logs full email addresses — personal data — when a userId alone would let someone look the record up in the system of record
It should use logger.debug instead of logger.info
Template literals can't include multiple variables
The word "changed" should be "updated" for consistency

hints: Beyond the searchability problem, look at what's actually inside the string — is any of it personal data that didn't need to be there?
What would a reader need to trace this event — the actual email addresses, or an identifier that points back to them?
explanation: Even fixed for structure — logger.info("email.changed", { userId, oldEmail, newEmail }) — this line still puts two real email addresses into log storage unnecessarily. A userId is sufficient to trace the event and look up the actual addresses in the system of record, which has proper access controls; the log store usually doesn't. This is the same principle as never logging a password: log an identifier, not the personal value it points to, unless there's a specific and justified reason the value itself needs to be searchable.

prompt: An assistant, asked to 'add logging to the login handler for debugging,' generates a line that logs the full request body on every failed login attempt. Explain specifically what's wrong with this, and rewrite the instruction you'd give the assistant instead so it doesn't happen again.
hints: What's likely sitting inside a login request body that shouldn't end up in a log store?
A good instruction names what to log and, just as importantly, what never to log.
explanation: Logging the full request body on a login attempt logs the plaintext password whenever the attempt includes one, which is present on essentially every failed login — turning the log store into a rolling record of real, reusable passwords, readable by anyone with log access, for as long as retention lasts. A better instruction is specific about both sides: 'log the username or user ID and the outcome (success/failure) of each login attempt; never log the request body or password field.' The fix isn't remembering to redact after the fact — it's not asking for a wholesale dump of unknown-shaped data in the first place, since generated code has no way to guess which of a request body's fields are safe.

prompt: A checkout endpoint's error logs are all individually well-written and searchable, but nobody notices the error rate climbing from 0.3% to 11% over twenty minutes until a customer complains. What's missing?

options.text: An aggregated metric — a count or rate over time — that would surface the trend as a moving number instead of requiring someone to notice a pattern across thousands of individual log lines
The log lines need to be written in red text so they stand out
The logs should be switched from info level to error level
Nothing — well-written logs are sufficient for catching any production problem

hints: Each individual error log is correct on its own — what would it take for a human to actually notice a rate, rather than an individual event?
What kind of number is built specifically to surface a trend as a line moving on a graph?
explanation: Well-written structured logs answer 'what happened in this one case' — they don't, on their own, surface 'the rate of this happening just jumped.' That's specifically what a metric is for: aggregating many individually-correct events into a count or rate over time, so a trend shows up as a number or a graph moving, instead of requiring a human to notice a pattern buried in a scrolling stream of individually normal-looking log lines.

prompt: Sort each proposed signal by whether it belongs in the RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) starter set for a request-handling endpoint, or is a second-layer signal worth adding later.

items.text: Requests per second on the /checkout endpoint
Error rate on the /checkout endpoint
p99 request duration on the /checkout endpoint
Garbage-collection pause count on the host
Connection-pool internals (idle vs. active connections)

hints: The RED set is specifically per-endpoint and tied directly to what a user experiences.
Second-layer signals are usually about the machine or runtime underneath, a step removed from the user.
explanation: Rate, errors, and duration, per endpoint, are directly tied to what a user experiences: how much traffic, how much of it fails, how long it takes. Garbage-collection pauses and connection-pool internals matter for diagnosing *why* duration or errors moved, but they're a layer removed from user impact — a service can have a GC pause spike with zero user-facing effect, or degrade badly with unremarkable GC stats. Start with RED; add the rest once you know it's needed to explain a RED signal that moved.

prompt: An on-call engineer mutes their phone before bed because a nightly "CPU above 70%" alert has fired for six months straight with no real impact every time. Three weeks later a genuine outage's alert goes unanswered. What actually caused the missed outage?

options.text: Repeated false-positive alerts trained the engineer to treat alerts from this system as probably nothing, including the one that mattered
The alerting system has a hard limit on how many alerts it can send per engineer
The genuine outage happened to occur during a scheduled maintenance window
CPU-based alerts are inherently less reliable than error-rate alerts

hints: This is a behavioral mechanism, not a technical one — what does firing routinely with no consequence teach a human, over six months?
Compare this to the flaky-test problem from the CI module — is the mechanism the same?
explanation: This is the same mechanism as a flaky required check eroding trust in CI: an alert that fires routinely and turns out to need no action teaches its responder, gradually and rationally, that alerts from this source are usually noise — and that lesson generalizes to every alert from the source, including the real one. The fix isn't a technical limit or a scheduling coincidence, it's that the alert should never have been symptom-shaped as "page a human" in the first place if it routinely required no action.

prompt: A team is deciding whether "disk usage above 60% on a volume that fills slowly over several weeks" should be a paging, wake-someone-up alert. True or false: this metric deserves a page.

config.statement: Slow, predictable disk-usage growth that takes weeks to become a real problem deserves an alert that pages an on-call engineer immediately.
config.rubric: Accepts justification naming that a slow, predictable trend doesn't require action right now — it belongs on a dashboard or a business-hours ticket, since paging trains the responder toward alert fatigue for a signal that was never actually urgent.

hints: Apply the test from the lesson: would this, if it fired at 3am, require a human to act right now?
What's the actual cost of waiting until business hours for something that takes weeks to become a real problem?
explanation: A slow, weeks-long trend fails the core test for a page: it doesn't require action right now, at 3am, by someone who was asleep. It belongs on a dashboard someone checks regularly, or a ticket filed during business hours — treating it as page-worthy trains the on-call engineer toward exactly the alert fatigue that makes them tune out real, urgent pages later. Urgency, not just importance, is what earns a wake-someone-up alert.

prompt: An on-call engineer, paged for a pricing bug in a generated module they've never closely read, opens the structured logs for the failed requests before opening any source file. What does this buy them that reading the source first wouldn't?

options.text: The logs narrow which specific code path is even involved, so they read a small relevant slice instead of the whole unfamiliar module
Nothing — they'll have to read the source eventually either way, so the order doesn't matter
It lets them skip reading the source code entirely, forever
Logs are always faster to read than source code, regardless of what they contain

hints: The point isn't avoiding reading code altogether — it's about how much of it you have to read, and which part.
What do the failed requests' shared field values tell you before you've opened anything?
explanation: Starting from logs doesn't eliminate the need to read source — it eliminates the need to read all of it blind. Someone who wrote the code has some intuition about where a bug probably lives; someone reading unfamiliar generated code under incident pressure has none. The failed requests' shared field values substitute for that missing intuition, narrowing 'read three hundred unfamiliar lines' down to 'read the fifteen that handle this one specific condition.'

prompt: Match each step of the hypothesis-first debugging sequence to what it specifically narrows for the next step.

pairs.right: Bounds when the problem started and how widespread it is

pairs.left: Pull structured logs for failures in that window
pairs.right: Bounds what's shared among the failing requests

pairs.left: Form a specific hypothesis from the shared field
pairs.right: Bounds which code path is even worth reading

pairs.left: Re-check the same metric after the fix ships
pairs.right: Confirms the fix actually worked, instead of just assuming it did

right: Confirms the on-call rotation schedule is correctly configured
Determines which team should be blamed for the incident

hints: Each step is evidence that narrows what the next step has to search — think about what gets smaller at each stage.
The last step closes the loop back to the first: the same signal that flagged the problem is what proves it's resolved.
explanation: Each step exists to narrow the next one's search space: the metric establishes when and how much, the logs establish what the failures share, the hypothesis establishes which narrow code path is worth reading at all, and — critically — the same metric that first surfaced the problem is what confirms the fix worked, rather than shipping a change and hoping. Skipping straight to reading source, or fixing without confirming via the metric, drops exactly the discipline this sequence is built around.

prompt: A generated log line reads console.log("cache miss"). It fires thousands of times a day, identically, for every one of dozens of different cache keys. What's the fastest fix that makes it actually useful?

options.text: Add the specific cache key as a structured field: log.debug("cache.miss", { key })
Change it to console.warn("cache miss") so it's more visible
Remove it entirely, since cache misses are expected behavior
Log it only once per server startup instead of on every miss

hints: What's the one thing that would let you tell which key is missing without reading source?
This is the same fix pattern as lesson one's payment example.
explanation: The line already correctly identifies the event type; what it's missing is the specific key involved, which is exactly the identifying detail that would let someone investigate why a particular key keeps missing (expired too fast? never warmed?) instead of just knowing that misses happen in general, which tells nobody anything actionable.

prompt: A team logs { userId, sessionToken, action } on every authenticated request "so we can trace a user's session if something goes wrong." True or false: sessionToken is safe to include because it's not a password.

config.statement: A session token is safe to log in full because, unlike a password, it isn't a secret.
config.rubric: Accepts justification naming that a session token is itself a credential — anyone who reads it from logs can impersonate that user's active session, making it as sensitive as a password for as long as the session is valid.

hints: What can someone do with a valid session token, if they read it from a log?
Is 'not literally a password' the same as 'not a secret'?
explanation: A session token is a bearer credential — whoever holds it can act as that user for as long as the session stays valid, exactly like a password would let them log in. Logging it in full means anyone with log access can hijack an active session without ever needing the actual password. The identifier that's safe to log here is the userId; the session token belongs in the same never-log category as a password, not a separate, safer one.

prompt: Sort each proposed alert by whether it's symptom-shaped (tied to user-facing impact, worth paging) or cause-shaped (a mechanism, worth a dashboard instead).

items.text: Checkout error rate above 5% for 5 minutes
p99 latency above 3s on a page users are actively waiting on
Database connection pool at 80% utilization
Nightly backup job's CPU spike, known to be harmless

hints: Ask of each one: if this fires at 3am, does it mean a user is affected right now?
A cause can be worth knowing about without being worth waking someone for.
explanation: Error rate and latency on a page a user is actively waiting on are direct, user-facing symptoms — exactly what justifies waking someone. Connection-pool utilization and a known-harmless CPU spike are causes or precursors, useful on a dashboard for understanding a symptom once one fires, but neither one alone means a user is affected right now, which is the actual bar for a page.

prompt: A metrics dashboard shows request rate holding steady, error rate holding steady at 0.2%, but p99 duration has crept from 200ms to 4 seconds over the past hour with no deploy in that window. Using only the RED metrics available (not source code), describe what you'd check next and why.
hints: Rate and errors haven't moved — what does that rule out?
What would you want to know about *which* requests are slow, not just that the average moved?
explanation: Steady rate and error rate rule out a traffic spike or a straightforward failure — this is specifically a duration problem, isolated to how long successful requests take, without any deploy to explain it. The next useful check is whether the slowdown is uniform across all requests or concentrated in a subset (a specific endpoint, a specific user segment, a specific downstream dependency) — which usually means looking at duration broken down by endpoint or checking whether a downstream service (database, third-party API) has itself gotten slower, since a code-level explanation is less likely without a corresponding deploy.

prompt: An incident is diagnosed to a specific discount-code handling bug using logs and metrics, and the fix ships. What's the last step this module's sequence says not to skip?

options.text: Watching the same error-rate metric that flagged the incident return to its normal baseline
Writing a full postmortem document before doing anything else
Deleting the logs that were used to diagnose the issue, now that it's resolved
Re-running the entire test suite twice for confidence

hints: What confirms a fix actually worked, versus just shipping and assuming?
This closes the loop back to whichever signal first surfaced the problem.
explanation: Confirming resolution against the same metric that first surfaced the problem is what turns 'we shipped a fix' into 'we know the fix worked' — without it, a fix that doesn't actually address the root cause can ship and get treated as resolved while the real error rate stays elevated. This is the step most likely to get skipped under the relief of having found a plausible cause.

prompt: Put these four items in order from most identifying-and-safe-to-log to least safe to log, for a checkout event.

items: full card number entered at checkout

hints: Which of these four carries zero personal or financial risk on its own?
Which one should never appear in a log line at all, regardless of position?
explanation: orderId, amountCents, and customerId are all safe, non-personal, non-secret identifiers or figures — freely loggable. A full card number is a secret with direct financial consequences if exposed and belongs in none of these positions; it should never be logged at all, which the exercise is really testing by putting it last among a set that's otherwise all fine to log in any order relative to each other.

prompt: A team adds forty different metrics to a new service on day one, including detailed garbage-collection internals, before adding a single error-rate metric. True or false: this is a reasonable instrumentation priority.

config.statement: Instrumenting forty detailed internal metrics before adding a basic error-rate metric is a reasonable way to prioritize a new service's observability.
config.rubric: Accepts justification naming that the RED set (rate, errors, duration) catches most user-facing problems and should come first — a large number of unwatched, low-level metrics often provides worse practical visibility than a small set someone actually checks.

hints: Which of the forty metrics is most directly tied to what a user experiences?
Does having more metrics automatically mean better visibility?
explanation: A service with a hundred half-watched metrics often has worse practical visibility than one with three that someone has built a habit of actually checking. Rate, errors, and duration per endpoint catch the large majority of user-facing problems and are cheap to reason about; detailed GC internals are a legitimate second-layer signal for diagnosing *why* a RED metric moved, not a substitute for having the RED metric in the first place.
